title: Susquehannock and the Ohio Valley Door
summary: The Susquehannock, an Iroquoian people of the lower Susquehanna, collapsed after Iroquois conquest around 1675, helping reopen the Ohio Valley.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Susquehannock](https://grokipedia.com/page/Susquehannock) never kept a town in Kentucky, but their fall helped decide who would claim it. They were an Iroquoian-speaking people of the lower Susquehanna valley, in what is now Pennsylvania and Maryland. English, Dutch, and Swedish traders knew them by other names too: Andaste, Minqua, and later Conestoga.

When Captain John Smith met them in 1608, they lived in large palisaded towns and farmed corn, beans, and squash. They were strong in the fur trade, and that strength put them in the path of the Haudenosaunee, the Five Nations of the Iroquois.

The long fight over furs and hunting ground is called the [Beaver Wars](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beaver_Wars). For decades the Susquehannock held their own. Then disease, war, and a break with their Maryland allies wore them down. By about 1675–76 their power was gone. Some survivors were taken in by the Iroquois. Others scattered south and west. A small group lived on at Conestoga in Pennsylvania until 1763, when a mob from Paxton killed the last of them.

Their fall mattered to Kentucky in a roundabout way. After the Beaver Wars the Iroquois said they had won the Ohio Valley by conquest, the hunting country south of the Ohio included. Few Iroquois lived there. Shawnee, Lenape, Mingo, Cherokee, and others hunted it, camped in it, and fought over it, and some of them disputed the Iroquois claim outright.

That claim did not stay on paper. At the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](/stories/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768/) in 1768, the Iroquois sold Britain their claim to the land south of the Ohio. Virginia hunters, surveyors, and settlers soon followed. The Shawnee, who had not signed, fought for that country in the years after.

The story of the [Iroquois Beaver Wars](/stories/iroquois-beaver-wars/) and the [Mingo camps south of the Ohio](/stories/mingo-camps-south-of-the-ohio/) picks up the thread from here. The Susquehannock are part of why the Kentucky country looked "empty" to the men who wrote the early deeds. It was not empty. It was contested.

## Kentucky today

No Susquehannock site is known in Kentucky. Their trace here is in the paper: the conquest claim sold at Fort Stanwix stands near the root of many early Kentucky land titles. The State Museum of Pennsylvania in Harrisburg displays Susquehannock pottery and tools from their homeland.
